Executive Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution
Foundational Statutory Authority under the Income Tax Act

Canada's primary fiscal mechanism for supporting private-sector innovation is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which operates through a dual-benefit statutory architecture codified in the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.). Unlike discretionary grant regimes that depend on competitive budget allocations and ministerial pre-approvals, the SR&ED program functions as an entitlement-based tax incentive embedded directly within the federal corporate and personal income tax systems. The program delivers two distinct yet interconnected statutory benefits to qualifying taxpayers carrying on business in Canada: first, an immediate 100% deduction of qualifying SR&ED expenditures against income for tax purposes—or an indefinite carryforward within a dedicated cumulative expenditure pool—under Section 37; and second, a refundable or non-refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from 15% to 35% of qualified SR&ED expenditures under Section 127 and Section 127.1.

The legal foundation of the Canadian R&D tax regime rests on four interconnected statutory pillars within the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. The threshold gateway is Subsection 248(1), which establishes the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This statutory definition encompasses basic research, applied research, and experimental development, alongside an enumerated list of eligible support work—specifically engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research—to the extent that such activities are commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core scientific or technological investigation.

Once work satisfies the threshold definition under subsection 248(1), Subsection 37(1) governs the deduction of domestic SR&ED expenditures in computing income from a business carried on in Canada. Paragraph 37(1)(a) permits a taxpayer to deduct current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada, encompassing expenditures directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), payments to certain approved research entities and consortia under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) and (i.1), and eligible payments to corporations resident in Canada. In parallel, paragraph 37(1)(b) governs the deduction of eligible SR&ED capital expenditures, which were abolished in 2014 but formally restored for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Unclaimed Section 37 deductions accumulate in a taxpayer's perpetual SR&ED expenditure pool and carry forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years, subject to the loss restriction event rules under paragraph 37(1)(h) and the corporate attribute trading anti-avoidance provisions of section 256.1 following an acquisition of control. Conversely, foreign SR&ED expenditures incurred outside Canada are excluded from the Section 37 pool and governed separately by subsection 37(2), which permits a current-year income deduction but restricts ITC eligibility strictly to permissible foreign salary allowances under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) and subsection 127(9).

The computation and application of the tax credit itself are governed by Subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), 127(10.2), and 127(10.6). Subsection 127(5) authorizes the deduction of earned SR&ED ITCs against a taxpayer's federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Subsection 127(9) codifies the operative statutory definitions, including "investment tax credit," "qualified expenditure," "prescribed proxy amount" (PPA), "contract payment," "government assistance," "non-government assistance," and "super-allowance benefit amount". Subsections 127(10.1), 127(10.2), and 127(10.6) establish the enhanced 35% ITC rate (comprising the 15% basic credit plus a 20% addition), define the annual expenditure limit, and prescribe the phase-out and allocation rules for associated corporations and consolidated corporate groups. Finally, Section 127.1 governs the cash refundability of unused ITCs earned in a taxation year, establishing differential refund rates of 100% or 40% depending on the claimant's corporate classification, whether the underlying expenditure is current or capital in nature, and whether the expenditure falls within the annual expenditure limit. To prevent a double fiscal benefit on the subsidized portion of an expenditure, paragraph 12(1)(t), subsection 13(7.1), and paragraph 37(1)(c) mandate that any SR&ED ITC claimed as a tax offset or received as a cash refund reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 expenditure pool or undepreciated capital cost (UCC) in the subsequent taxation year, or is included directly in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t) to the extent the pool becomes negative.

body.text: The 2024–2026 Legislative Modernization: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Budget 2026

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential legislative transformation since the 2012–2014 federal budget contractions. Recognizing that declining business enterprise R&D (BERD) intensity and domestic intellectual property migration threatened Canadian productivity growth, the Department of Finance Canada initiated a comprehensive two-phase public consultation process in early 2024. The first phase of consultations ran from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, inviting stakeholder submissions on modernizing the statutory definition of SR&ED, reforming eligibility criteria and overall program architecture, improving complementarity with direct innovation grants, and ensuring domestic retention of intellectual property through a potential patent box regime. In Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation (tabled April 16, 2024), the federal government launched the second phase of consultations—which ran through May 27, 2024—and committed an initial fiscal envelope of $600 million over four years starting in 2025–26, with $150 million per year ongoing, to fund targeted SR&ED program enhancements.

On December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024), substantially expanding the federal funding commitment to $1.9 billion over six years and announcing concrete legislative reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024). Although the subsequent prorogation of Parliament until March 24, 2025, following the resignation of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau temporarily delayed the passage of implementing bills, the federal government reaffirmed and further expanded these SR&ED enhancements in the 2025 and 2026 federal budgets. Specifically, while the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, subsequent Budget 2025 measures (tabled November 4, 2025)—enacted by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3 (Bill C-15, Royal Assent March 26, 2026), reflected in the Canada Revenue Agency's (CRA) updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and mirrored in provincial implementation statutes such as British Columbia's Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026—further raised the annual expenditure limit to $6.0 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

This multi-stage legislative evolution altered four structural parameters of Canadian R&D tax law for taxation years commencing after December 15, 2024. First, the annual qualified expenditure threshold eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate increased from $3.0 million (applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024) to $4.5 million under the initial FES 2024 proposal, and ultimately to $6.0 million under the enacted 2025–2026 framework. At the $6.0 million ceiling, a qualifying corporation can earn up to $2.1 million annually in enhanced 35% federal SR&ED ITCs, compared to $1.05 million under the legacy $3.0 million limit and $1.575 million under the interim $4.5 million FES 2024 proposal. Second, for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range—over which the expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis to nil—was raised from the historic $10 million to $50 million bracket to a wider $15 million to $75 million bracket.

Third, the post-December 15, 2024 reforms eliminated the long-standing "IPO penalty" by extending eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to the annual expenditure limit. Under the prior law, a domestic technology company that completed a public listing or became controlled by a Canadian public company immediately lost CCPC status, forfeiting the 35% refundable credit and dropping to a 15% non-refundable rate. For ECPCs, the expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis when the consolidated corporate group's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years is between $15 million and $75 million. Simultaneously, CCPCs were granted a statutory election to compute their expenditure limit phase-out using this three-year average gross revenue structure instead of taxable capital employed in Canada, allowing capital-intensive, pre-revenue or low-revenue CCPCs to preserve their full enhanced credit despite raising large equity or debt financing rounds. Fourth, reversing the 2014 repeal of capital costs, the federal government restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs for both the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC, effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), and for lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024. Building on these enacted reforms, Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) proposes, for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026, to extend SR&ED eligibility to tests, technological validations and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for the initial approval or certification needed to commercialize a product or process, where directly related to an eligible SR&ED project, and to the costs of registering and maintaining intellectual property protection (patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights and copyrighted software) for IP developed in an eligible SR&ED project.
Federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics
Enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit for CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

The federal SR&ED program employs a two-tier credit architecture designed to maximize working-capital liquidity for small and medium-sized domestic innovators while providing baseline tax offsets for large enterprises and foreign-controlled subsidiaries. Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, the enhanced federal ITC rate is 35%, representing the sum of the 15% basic ITC and a 20% statutory enhancement.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, entitlement to the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to corporations that qualified throughout the taxation year as Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) within the meaning of subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act—namely, private Canadian corporations that are not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations, or by any combination thereof. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, entitlement to the enhanced 35% rate applies to both qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs). An ECPC is defined as a corporation that, throughout the taxation year, is resident in Canada, has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada (or has elected, or been designated by the Minister, to be a public corporation), and is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

body.text: Phase-Out Mechanics: Taxable Capital Employed in Canada vs. Consolidated Gross Revenue Election

Under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act, the annual expenditure limit must be allocated among all associated CCPCs (within the meaning of section 256) or among all members of a consolidated corporate group for ECPCs, and is prorated according to the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 (or 366 in a leap year) for short taxation years.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to contract when the taxable capital employed in Canada—computed under Part I.3 of the Income Tax Act (sections 181.2 to 181.4) and detailed in CRA Interpretation Bulletin IT-532—of the corporation and all associated CCPCs for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $10,000,000, and is reduced to nil once prior-year taxable capital reaches $50,000,000. The statutory expenditure limit for pre-December 16, 2024 taxation years is expressed mathematically as:

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (of the corporation or its associated group) is $10,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the lower phase-out threshold under the taxable capital method increases to $15,000,000 and the upper elimination threshold increases to $75,000,000, creating a $60,000,000 straight-line phase-out span. Under the enacted $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit (which superseded the initial $4,500,000 FES 2024 proposal), the expenditure limit diminishes by $1 for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (of the corporation or its associated group) is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Under the initial $4,500,000 expenditure limit proposed in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement prior to the Budget 2025/2026 increase to $6,000,000, the numerator base was $4,500,000, phasing out at $0.075 per dollar of taxable capital between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000.

Because public corporations do not track CCPC-style Part I.3 taxable capital for small business deduction purposes—and because capital-intensive R&D companies in biotechnology, clean energy, quantum computing, and hardware manufacturing routinely raise tens of millions of dollars in preferred equity or venture debt (which directly inflates Part I.3 taxable capital employed in Canada via share capital, retained earnings, and indebtedness) years before achieving commercial revenue—the post-December 15, 2024 regime introduced an alternative Gross Revenue Phase-Out Structure. This revenue-based phase-out formula under subsection 127(10.6) is mandatory for ECPCs and available by election to CCPCs under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32). Under this method, the expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years lies between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if average annual revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (of the corporation or, where applicable, its consolidated or associated group) is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000.

According to the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, the corporate group aggregation rules governing the three-year average gross revenue calculation operate differently depending on whether the claimant is an ECPC or an electing CCPC. For an ECPC, the expenditure limit is shared among all members of a consolidated corporate group that prepare consolidated financial statements presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as a single economic entity. The annual revenue reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group is used to calculate the three-year average annual revenue and resulting expenditure limit. If an entity joins or leaves the consolidated group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in its consolidated financial statements for the year in question. Conversely, when a CCPC elects to use the gross revenue method and is associated with other corporations, the calculation requires summing the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation that is a member of the associated group for the taxation year in question across the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year lookback period.
Basic 15% Investment Tax Credit, Carryback, Carryforward, and Recapture Rules

All qualified SR&ED expenditures that are not eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC—including expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-ECPC public corporations, and CCPC or ECPC expenditures that exceed the corporation's annual expenditure limit—earn the basic federal ITC rate of 15% under subsection 127(9).

The utilization and cash refundability of earned ITCs follow a strict statutory ordering under subsections 127(5) and 127.1(1) of the Income Tax Act. First, all ITCs earned in the taxation year must be applied under subsection 127(5) to offset the taxpayer's federal Part I income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year. Second, any unclaimed balance of ITCs earned in the year remaining after offsetting current-year Part I tax is eligible for a cash refund under section 127.1 according to tiered statutory percentages. Specifically, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC receives a 100% cash refund on the unclaimed balance of ITCs earned at the enhanced 35% rate in respect of qualified SR&ED expenditures of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount). By contrast, a 40% cash refund applies to three distinct categories of unclaimed current-year ITCs: (i) ITCs earned by a qualifying CCPC or ECPC at the enhanced 35% rate in respect of qualified SR&ED capital expenditures (for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024); (ii) ITCs earned at the basic 15% rate on qualified expenditures (both current and capital) by a "qualifying corporation" (defined as a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada do not exceed the statutory qualifying thresholds); and (iii) ITCs earned at the basic 15% rate by unincorporated individuals and certain trusts. All ITCs earned at the 15% basic rate by non-CCPC corporations—including ECPCs on expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit, foreign-controlled corporations, and large CCPCs exceeding the qualifying thresholds—are 0% refundable (non-refundable).

Any portion of an earned ITC that is neither refunded in cash nor used to offset current-year Part I tax payable may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax payable in those years. Once an ITC is carried back or carried forward from the taxation year in which it was earned, it permanently loses its refundable status and may only be utilized as a non-refundable tax offset. Furthermore, under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the Income Tax Act, if a taxpayer disposes of, or converts to commercial use, a property whose cost was previously included in qualified SR&ED expenditures—whether a transformed material claimed as a current expenditure or SR&ED capital property acquired after December 15, 2024—the taxpayer is subject to mandatory ITC recapture. The recaptured amount, calculated as the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of conversion to commercial use), is added directly to the taxpayer's federal Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion, while simultaneously adjusting the capital cost allowance (CCA) class or unclaimed Section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Pool Computation
Direct Labour, Foreign R&D Permissible Limits, and Specified Employees

Salaries and wages constitute the primary cost driver of qualified SR&ED expenditures across Canadian industry. Under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, eligible labour expenditures comprise salaries, wages, and taxable benefits (as reported on T4 slips under sections 5, 6, and 7 of the Income Tax Act, together with the employer's share of Canada Pension Plan (CPP) or Québec Pension Plan (QPP) contributions, Employment Insurance (EI) premiums, provincial payroll health taxes, and workers' compensation board assessments when the Traditional Method is elected) paid or incurred for employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED.

To withstand a CRA financial review, labour claims must adhere to four statutory limitations. First, under the Directly Engaged Allocation Rule, technical personnel—including scientists, engineers, software developers, laboratory technicians, and hands-on first-line technical supervisors who provide direct technical guidance rather than purely administrative management—are eligible in exact proportion to the working time they devote to eligible SR&ED activities (basic research, applied research, experimental development, and commensurate support work). Where an employee devotes 90% or more ("all or substantially all") of their working time in the taxation year to SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages may be included in the SR&ED expenditure pool. Clerical, administrative, legal, finance, marketing, and human resources personnel are excluded from direct SR&ED labour, as their indirect support functions are remunerated through the Prescribed Proxy Amount under the Proxy Method.

Second, strict statutory caps apply to Specified Employees, defined in subsection 248(1) as any employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who owns, directly or indirectly at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation. For specified employees, all bonuses and remuneration based on corporate profits are completely excluded from SR&ED eligibility, and total deductible SR&ED salary and wages in the Section 37 pool cannot exceed five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the year. When the taxpayer elects the Proxy Method, the salary of each specified employee included in the proxy salary base is further restricted under Regulation 2900(7) to 75% of the employee's net eligible salary and wages (excluding taxable benefits, bonuses, and unpaid remuneration), subject to an absolute ceiling of 2.5 times the YMPE prorated by days of employment.

Third, under the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule in subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary, wage, or accrued remuneration that remains unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, and may only be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid. Fourth, under the Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salary Rule in subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) and subsection 127(9), while SR&ED must generally be conducted within Canada to earn ITCs, a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada may include salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED carried on outside Canada, provided the foreign work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer as an integral component of a Canadian SR&ED project and the remuneration is not subject to an income or profits tax in the foreign country. The maximum permissible foreign SR&ED salary is capped at 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.
Overhead Allocation: The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers claiming SR&ED in Canada must make an annual election on Form T661 (Line 160) to compute their SR&ED overhead and other expenditures using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Once filed for a taxation year, this election is irrevocable for that year.

body.text: For the vast majority of labour-intensive Canadian R&D claimants—particularly in software development, artificial intelligence, life sciences, and engineering services—the Proxy Method generates a substantially larger ITC base while insulating the claimant from the onerous documentation requirements of substantiating itemized overhead allocations during a CRA financial review. Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is a notional statutory figure added directly to qualified expenditures on Line 502 of Form T661, it earns the full 35% enhanced refundable ITC (yielding an effective cash subsidy of 19.25% on top of the 35% credit on direct Canadian R&D salaries, for a combined federal ITC of 54.25% of eligible Canadian R&D wages before provincial credits). Conversely, the Traditional Method is economically advantageous only for facility-intensive or heavy industrial claimants that employ a small internal R&D workforce while incurring massive, verifiable incremental overhead costs—such as dedicated shop-floor utilities, specialized cloud computing infrastructure, or non-salary support costs—that exceed 55% of their direct Canadian R&D salary base.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Materials Consumed or Transformed

Beyond internal salaries and overhead, the Section 37 expenditure pool and Section 127 ITC base incorporate three primary external expenditure categories: materials consumed or transformed, subcontractor payments, and third-party payments.

Under Regulation 2900(2), physical materials qualify for SR&ED inclusion if they are either materials consumed (rendered virtually value-less, destroyed, or exhausted during the course of experimental trials) or materials transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during the systematic investigation). Supplies that are not physically incorporated into the experimental work or consumed directly in the tests are treated as overhead (covered by the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method or itemized under the Traditional Method). If an experimental prototype or transformed material whose cost was claimed for SR&ED is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the ITC recapture provisions under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) apply to recover the credit based on the lesser of the original material cost and the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at conversion.

When a taxpayer engages a taxable Canadian supplier to perform SR&ED in Canada on its behalf under an arm's-length subcontract, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in computing the Section 37 pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract payment may be included in the "qualified expenditure" base for Section 127 ITC calculation (reflecting the statutory 20% reduction enacted in 2013 to exclude the contractor's assumed commercial profit markup). To qualify under subsection 37(1), the payer must control the technical specifications, assume the financial and technological risk, and retain ownership or exploitation rights to the resulting intellectual property, while the work performed by the subcontractor must constitute either a standalone SR&ED project or eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) commensurate with the payer's own Canadian SR&ED project. Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length party, the contract payment itself does not qualify for ITCs in the hands of the payer; instead, the non-arm's-length performer may claim the underlying actual SR&ED expenditures it incurred, or the parties may execute a joint agreement to transfer qualified expenditures (Form T1146) up to the statutory transfer ceiling. Similarly, third-party payments made to approved Canadian universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED research consortia for SR&ED carried out in Canada that relates to the taxpayer's business (where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results) are 100% deductible under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) or (i.1) and are included at 80% in the federal Section 127 ITC base (reported on Form T1263).
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024 Regime)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures—encompassing depreciable property such as laboratory instrumentation, environmental test chambers, pilot-scale manufacturing machinery, cleanroom fabrication tools, and dedicated on-premise AI GPU server clusters—along with capital lease costs were statutorily excluded from both the Section 37 SR&ED deduction and the Section 127 ITC. Throughout that ten-year period, taxpayers could only recover capital equipment costs through standard multi-year Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules under paragraph 20(1)(a).

Pursuant to the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and subsequent enacting legislation, the eligibility of capital expenditures was fully restored for both the Section 37 deduction against income and the Section 127 ITC components of the SR&ED program, effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and, in the case of lease costs, for amounts that first become payable after December 15, 2024.

The restored capital expenditure regime reinstates the pre-2014 statutory rules under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9). To qualify as an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure, the depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) must satisfy the strict "All or Substantially All" (90% or more) qualification test at the time it becomes available for use. Specifically, the taxpayer must demonstrate that the capital asset is intended to either: (i) be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time throughout its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada; or (ii) consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. Because the restored rules revert to the pre-2014 framework without reinstating the historical shared-use equipment rules (which prior to 2014 had allowed partial 25% or 50% ITCs on equipment used between 50% and 90% for R&D), equipment that is split between commercial production and R&D without reaching the 90% SR&ED operating-time threshold does not qualify for the SR&ED ITC. Lease payments for tangible property (other than a building) that first become payable after December 15, 2024, similarly qualify if the leased property meets the 90% SR&ED use test during the lease period (under the Traditional Method) or if the asset would have qualified as SR&ED capital property had it been purchased directly.

With respect to credit rates and refundability, qualifying SR&ED capital expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC within its $6.0 million annual expenditure limit earn the 35% enhanced ITC, while capital expenditures above the limit or incurred by other corporations earn the 15% basic ITC. However, a critical statutory distinction governs cash refundability under section 127.1: whereas unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% rate on current expenditures are 100% refundable, unclaimed ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate on capital expenditures are 40% refundable (resulting in a maximum immediate cash refund of 14% of the capital cost for a non-taxpaying CCPC or ECPC, with the remaining 21% of the ITC available to offset current-year Part I tax or carry back 3 years / carry forward 20 years). If SR&ED capital property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, statutory recapture rules apply under subsections 127(27)–(35) and section 13 to claw back both the previously claimed CCA or Section 37 capital deduction and the SR&ED ITC.

For capital assets that do not meet the 90% SR&ED use threshold (such as dual-use production/R&D equipment), Canadian tax law provides complementary accelerated depreciation incentives. The 2024 Fall Economic Statement fully reinstated the Accelerated Investment Incentive—allowing businesses to claim up to three times the normal first-year CCA on eligible depreciable property acquired on or after January 1, 2025, and available for use before 2030 (phasing out between 2030 and 2033)—alongside 100% Immediate Expensing for manufacturing and processing machinery and equipment (CCA Class 53), clean energy generation and conservation equipment (CCA Classes 43.1 and 43.2), and zero-emission vehicles. In addition, Budget 2024 enacted 100% immediate expensing for productivity-enhancing assets in CCA Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), CCA Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment), and CCA Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software) acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027.
Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and the Super-Allowance Benefit

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraphs 37(1)(c), (d), and (d.1) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, contract payments, or super-allowance benefit amounts that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the time of filing its income tax return for the year.

Government assistance is broadly defined in subsection 127(9) to encompass any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance received from a federal, provincial, or municipal government or public authority. Crucially, this definition includes all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants—such as the Ontario OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC, the Québec CRIC, the British Columbia SR&ED credit, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), and the Atlantic/Prairie provincial R&D credits—as well as direct federal innovation grants such as National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) contributions. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance in the year the underlying R&D expenditure is incurred, the amount of the provincial credit earned must be deducted on Line 513 of federal Form T661, thereby "grinding" down the net qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the federal Section 127 ITC. If a taxpayer subsequently repays government assistance that previously reduced its qualified expenditures, the repaid amount is added back to the qualified expenditure pool in the year of repayment.

Similarly, a contract payment—defined in subsection 127(9) as an amount payable by a taxable Canadian supplier or a federal/provincial government body for SR&ED to be performed for or on behalf of that payer—must be deducted by the performing contractor from its qualified SR&ED expenditures so that two Canadian taxpayers cannot claim SR&ED ITCs on the exact same R&D work. However, payments received from foreign (non-resident) clients that do not carry on business in Canada are excluded from the statutory definition of "contract payment" under subsection 127(9). Consequently, a Canadian engineering, contract research organization (CRO), or software development firm performing R&D in Canada under contract for a foreign corporation is not required to reduce its qualified expenditures by the foreign contract revenue, and may claim the full federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits on its underlying Canadian costs. Finally, under paragraph 37(1)(d.1) and subsection 127(9), if a province provides a tax deduction in respect of SR&ED that exceeds 100% of the actual expenditure incurred, the resulting super-allowance benefit amount must also be deducted from the federal Section 37 pool and qualified expenditure base.
Scientific and Technological Eligibility Criteria and Jurisprudential Precedents
Statutory Definition under Subsection 248(1) and Excluded Activities

Whether a technical project qualifies for SR&ED incentives is governed by the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and administered in accordance with the CRA's Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and structures qualifying activities into four statutory limbs. Basic research under paragraph (a) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Applied research under paragraph (b) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development under paragraph (c)—which accounts for more than 95% of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada—comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Once a core project qualifies under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), eligible support work under paragraph (d) encompasses work in respect of engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) establish an explicit statutory exclusion list. Even if performed by qualified engineers or scientists as part of a broader commercial product launch, the following activities are statutorily excluded from SR&ED: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; and (k) routine data collection.
The Five-Question Legal Framework: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

The authoritative judicial test for determining whether claimed activities satisfy the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) was articulated by Chief Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), and formally adopted as the binding national standard by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393.

In Northwest Hydraulic, Chief Justice Bowman synthesized the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) into five cumulative questions, each of which must be answered in the affirmative on a balance of probabilities for a project to qualify as SR&ED:

items: Question 1 — Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Chief Justice Bowman explained that "routine engineering" encompasses techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If the resolution of a technical problem is predictable using established engineering methodologies, off-the-shelf vendor specifications, or standard computational algorithms, no technological uncertainty exists—even if the implementation is complex, time-consuming, or commercially risky. Genuine technological uncertainty arises either when it is uncertain whether a specific technical objective can be achieved at all given the underlying laws of science or limits of current technology, or when the taxpayer faces system-level uncertainty regarding which technological architecture or methodology will satisfy conflicting performance parameters (such as latency, throughput, thermal stability, or shelf-life) without degrading core functionality.

Question 2 — Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This criterion requires a structured five-stage intellectual progression: (i) rigorous observation of the subject matter of the problem; (ii) formulation of a clear technical objective; (iii) identification and explicit articulation of the underlying technological uncertainty; (iv) formulation of one or more testable hypotheses specifically designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty; and (v) methodical, systematic testing of those hypotheses through experiment or analysis.

Question 3 — Total Discipline of the Scientific Method: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of the hypotheses? What separates qualifying SR&ED from intuition, unguided trial-and-error ("tinkering"), or routine debugging is the systematic, iterative cycle of hypothesis formulation, controlled experimentation or mathematical/computational analysis, observation of empirical results, causal evaluation of why a test succeeded or failed, and systematic modification of the hypothesis in light of those findings.

Question 4 — Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement? A technological advancement represents an advancement in the general stock of technological understanding known to competent professionals in the relevant industry—not merely a company-specific learning curve or the adoption of existing industry knowledge. Crucially, Chief Justice Bowman held that the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement if the experimental process generates new scientific or engineering knowledge proving that a plausible technical path cannot work under given constraints; commercial viability or technical success of the final product is never a prerequisite for SR&ED eligibility.

Question 5 — Contemporaneous Record Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results kept as the work progressed? Contemporaneous documentation provides the objective evidentiary trail confirming that a systematic scientific investigation actually occurred as the work unfolded, rather than being retroactively fabricated during claim preparation.

body.text: In its administrative guidance (Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and the Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors), the CRA maps the five Northwest Hydraulic questions directly into a two-requirement framework—referred to as the "Why" and "How" requirements—which both emanate from subsection 248(1). The "Why" requirement encompasses Questions 1 and 4, asking whether the work was conducted for the purpose of achieving scientific or technological advancement by resolving an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty. The "How" requirement encompasses Questions 2, 3, and 5, asking whether the work was executed as a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis, substantiated by contemporaneous evidence.
Evolving Jurisprudence on Contemporaneous Documentation, Applied Engineering, and Software

Subsequent jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) has clarified how the Northwest Hydraulic framework applies to evidentiary disputes, applied manufacturing, food science, and software engineering.

body.text: Three foundational legal principles emerge from these judicial precedents for tax auditors and corporate claimants. First, with respect to the evidentiary status of contemporaneous documentation, CRA auditors frequently attempt to disallow SR&ED claims automatically whenever a claimant lacks formal laboratory notebooks or standardized test reports. In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, relying on Justice Archambault's reasoning in 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] A.C.I. No. 478 (TCC), the Tax Court of Canada held unequivocally that the existence of contemporaneous written documents with specific content is not a mandatory legal condition precedent for SR&ED recognition under the Income Tax Act or the Income Tax Regulations. As the Court emphasized, "in tax matters, taxpayers cannot be required to do more than the obligations the Act imposes on them". While a taxpayer lacking contemporaneous written records places itself in a precarious evidentiary position when contesting a ministerial refusal, it remains legally permissible to prove that systematic hypothesis testing occurred through credible oral testimony and surrounding factual evidence. Moreover, in Les Abeilles, the Tax Court rebuked a CRA Scientific Advisor (Mr. Kooi) who testified as an expert witness for conflating his administrative audit role with his duty to the Court, noting that an expert witness must offer an independent professional opinion on technological uncertainty rather than mechanically applying internal CRA policy manuals.

Second, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, and subsequent 2022 Federal Court of Appeal software rulings, taxpayers argued that the five-part Northwest Hydraulic test was merely judicial guidance rather than a mandatory statutory requirement under subsection 248(1), particularly in iterative software engineering and shop-floor manufacturing environments. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected that argument, holding that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are mandatory legal prerequisites inherent in subsection 248(1), while simultaneously instructing the Tax Court that the test must be applied in a flexible manner suitable for applied sciences and taking into consideration the taxpayer's specific business environment.

Third, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC), the Tax Court addressed the recurring audit dispute over where "routine engineering" ends and "technological uncertainty" begins in applied product and process development. In Manning Canning, the taxpayer sought during its 2020 taxation year to develop a canned, shelf-stable beverage containing cold-pressed fruit juice as a primary ingredient—a product that did not exist on the market because unpasteurized fruit is inherently contaminated with yeast, bacteria, and mould ("dirty by nature"). The Minister of National Revenue denied the claim on the ground that mitigating microbial spoilage in beverages involved only routine food engineering and standard preservation procedures. The Tax Court allowed the taxpayer's appeal, finding on a balance of probabilities that because standard thermal pasteurization or chemical preservation techniques would destroy the organoleptic and nutritional profile of cold-pressed juice, the taxpayer faced a genuine technological uncertainty that could not be resolved by routine engineering, and had systematically formulated and tested hypotheses in accordance with the scientific method (citing Northwest Hydraulic, C.W. Agencies, Clevor Technologies, and Joel Theatrical Rigging).
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly every Canadian province and territory supplements the federal SR&ED program with its own statutory corporate income tax credit or tax-system grant. With the exception of Québec (which is administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (which is administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance — Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA)), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) under federal-provincial tax collection agreements and are claimed on dedicated schedules filed directly with the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

body.text: Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all of which are processed by the CRA and require the claimant to maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario and file a federal Form T661. The flagship small-business incentive is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on T2 Schedule 566. For taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016, the OITC provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000 (reduced from the pre-June 1, 2016 rate of 10% and maximum credit of $300,000). Although the March 28, 2018 Ontario Budget had proposed a tiered OITC rate rising to 12% for firms with an Ontario R&D-to-gross-revenue ratio of 20% or higher, that proposal was not enacted following the June 2018 change in provincial government, leaving the statutory OITC rate at a flat 8%.

Crucially, tax auditors must note that Ontario did not align the OITC expenditure limit or phase-out thresholds with the federal 2024–2026 expansions; instead, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit (shared among associated corporations) continues to phase out on a straight-line basis if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. However, because Ontario defines "qualified expenditure" directly by reference to subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, official Government of Ontario guidance confirms that OITC qualified expenditures automatically incorporate 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (alongside 100% of current expenditures and 40% of pre-2014 capital expenditures, while excluding capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024).

Alongside the OITC, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC)—claimed on T2 Schedule 508—provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% in June 2016) to all eligible corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario, net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed on those same expenditures. Unused ORDTC credits may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable, or a loss-making corporation may formally waive the ORDTC in a given year so as not to trigger an immediate government assistance grind under subsection 127(9) against its 35% refundable federal SR&ED credit. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC)—claimed on T2 Schedules 568 and 569—provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on up to $20,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures (maximum $4,000,000 annual credit) incurred under an eligible research contract with an approved Ontario post-secondary institution, hospital research institute, or prescribed non-profit research centre.
Québec: Elimination of Legacy Credits and the New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

Québec administers an autonomous corporate and personal income tax system under the Taxation Act (Québec), enforced by Revenu Québec. In the Québec Budget 2025–2026 (tabled March 25, 2025), the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentives effective for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025.

For taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec formally eliminated its five legacy R&D and industrial design tax credits: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7-V), which previously offered a 14% basic refundable credit and up to a 30% enhanced refundable credit for SMEs with consolidated worldwide assets below $50 million (phasing out to 14% at $75 million) on Québec R&D wages and 50% of arm's-length subcontractor payments above an indexed per-employee "exclusion threshold"; (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V); (3) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V, which required an annual qualification certificate from the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie (MEIE)); (4) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V); and (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services and industrial design tax credit provisions. Corporations, partnerships, individuals (on Line 462), and trusts whose taxation years or fiscal periods began on or before March 25, 2025, continue to claim those legacy credits for that transitional period under the prior rules and forms (accompanied by Form RD-222-V, Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures).

Replacing the abolished legacy credits for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, is the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC). Under the new statutory regime, unincorporated individuals and personal returns (Line 462) are no longer eligible; the CRIC can only be claimed by qualified corporations and corporations that are members of a qualified partnership that carry on a business in Québec and maintain an establishment in Québec. Tax-exempt entities, Crown corporations, and corporations controlled by prescribed research entities remain excluded.

In a major structural expansion beyond the traditional boundaries of federal subsection 248(1), the Québec CRIC subsidizes both R&D activities and pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation or partnership. Pre-commercialization activities encompass downstream technological validation and market-readiness steps that are excluded from federal SR&ED, including regulatory testing, product certification and homologation, industrial design and product engineering for manufacturability, and commercial pilot prototyping. Eligible CRIC expenditures encompass four categories: (i) salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec; (ii) consideration paid to subcontractors; (iii) payments to eligible universities, public research centres, or research consortia; and (iv) capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property used in Québec R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

Furthermore, Québec repealed the $50 million to $75 million consolidated worldwide asset phase-out so that mid-sized and large enterprises can access the enhanced rate on their initial spending slice. Under the CRIC rate structure, every qualified corporation (or associated group sharing the limit) earns a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (above the applicable exclusion threshold), and a 20% fully refundable tax credit (increased from the legacy 14% basic rate) on all eligible expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 limit. To claim the credit with the CO-17 corporate income tax return, corporations must file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC)), accompanied where applicable by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T (Agreement Regarding the Expenditure Limit for the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization) and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T (Information Regarding the Pre-Commercialization Component of the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization), alongside Form RD-222-V. Under the Québec Budget 2025 compliance rules, failure to file the mandatory new Québec reporting form triggers a penalty of $500 per month (or part of a month) up to 24 months (maximum $12,000), which is doubled to $24,000 if the entity fails to meet the deadline after receiving formal notice from Revenu Québec.
British Columbia: Harmonization with Federal ECPCs, $6 Million Cap, and Capital Expenditure Restoration

Governed by Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (British Columbia)—previously extended through August 31, 2027, by the 2022 BC Budget and made permanent by Bill 2, Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (S.B.C. 2026, c. 5), which removed the credit's expiry date—the British Columbia Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit provides a 10% credit on BC qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a qualifying corporation with a permanent establishment in British Columbia.

As confirmed by official Government of British Columbia tax guidance updated in April 2026, British Columbia fully harmonized its provincial SR&ED regime with the federal 2024–2026 legislative reforms for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Specifically, qualifying corporations that are CCPCs or Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) may claim a 10% fully refundable tax credit on the lesser of their SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the taxation year or their federal expenditure limit as determined under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the federal Income Tax Act. Because the federal expenditure limit increased from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the maximum annual refundable BC SR&ED credit doubled from $300,000 to $600,000, while automatically adopting the expanded $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out (and the three-year average gross revenue phase-out for ECPCs and electing CCPCs). In addition, British Columbia restored the eligibility of capital expenditures as BC qualified expenditures for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

All other qualifying corporations—including foreign-controlled corporations, active corporate members of partnerships claiming their proportionate share of partnership BC SR&ED expenditures, and CCPCs or ECPCs with BC qualified expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit—are entitled to a 10% non-refundable BC SR&ED tax credit to offset BC corporate income tax payable (with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward), or may formally renounce the non-refundable credit to avoid grinding down their federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool. The credit is claimed by filing Form T666 (British Columbia (BC) Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit) and entering the non-refundable credit on Line 659 and the refundable credit on Line 674 of T2 Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations) no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Two-Step Iterative Grind Calculation

Following the 2019 elimination of the former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit, the Government of Alberta enacted Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act effective January 1, 2021, establishing the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG). Although styled as a "grant," the IEG is legally a refundable corporate income tax credit administered directly by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance — Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) in accordance with Information Circular IEG-1R5 (and predecessor circulars IEG-1R1 and IEG-1R4) and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant.

The IEG provides up to a 20% fully refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta (for a maximum annual refundable payment of $800,000) through a two-tier incremental rate formula. First, a corporation's base level of spending (base amount) is determined by calculating the average of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (specifically, the expenditures in respect of SR&ED carried out in Alberta that were included on Line 559 of federal Form T661) over the two immediately preceding taxation years. If the corporation had no eligible Alberta R&D expenditures in the preceding two years, its base amount is nil ($0), and if it incurred eligible expenditures in only one of the two preceding years, the total is still divided by 2 (for example, $0 in Year 1 and $20,000 in Year 2 produces a base amount of $10,000). Under the Part I Calculation on Form AT29 (Line 110), the corporation earns an 8% base payment on the lesser of its current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditures and its maximum expenditure limit ($4,000,000). Under the Part II Calculation on Form AT29 (Line 125), the corporation earns an additional 12% incremental payment—bringing the combined rate to 20%—on the portion of its current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (up to the $4,000,000 expenditure limit) that exceeds its two-year average base spending level. Consequently, a startup or first-time Alberta R&D claimant with a $0 base amount earns the full 20% refundable credit on 100% of its eligible Alberta R&D spending up to $4,000,000.

Unlike the federal enhanced 35% rate, the Alberta IEG is open to all corporations (including foreign-controlled subsidiaries and public corporations) that maintain a permanent establishment in Alberta, provided their prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (shared across associated corporations) is less than $50,000,000. The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis for corporations (and associated corporate groups, per the retroactive January 1, 2021 technical amendments announced in December 2023) with prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, and is reduced to nil at $50,000,000 or more.

Because the Alberta IEG constitutes provincial government assistance that must be deducted on Line 513 of federal Form T661—and because Alberta defines eligible IEG expenditures directly from the net federal qualified expenditures on Line 559/557 of Form T661 after deducting Line 513 assistance—TRA mandates a specific Two-Step Calculation Process in the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant. In Step 1 (Preliminary Calculation of the IEG), the claimant completes AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) using its unreduced federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (setting Line 011 of Form AT29 to zero) before deducting the IEG as provincial government assistance on federal Form T661, arriving at the preliminary IEG on Line 130 of Form AT29. In Step 2 (Final Calculation of the IEG), the claimant enters that preliminary IEG amount from Line 130 of Form AT29 onto Line 513 of federal Form T661 as "provincial government assistance," which reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 559/557 of Form T661. The claimant then enters the reduced federal qualified expenditure total onto Line 003 of Form AT29 to compute the final Net IEG on Line 134 of Form AT29, which is carried to Line 129 of the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1). Claimants must submit Form AT29 and Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) within 18 months of the taxation year-end (and electronically via Net File for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024), and TRA formally issues the IEG refund only after receiving confirmation from the CRA of the assessed federal SR&ED expenditures.
Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon

Across the Prairie and Atlantic provinces and the Northern territories, provincial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA and harmonized directly with the federal definition of qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9). In Saskatchewan, under section 7.7 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (claimed on T2 Schedule 403), corporations with a permanent establishment in the province earn a 10% tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Saskatchewan (historically enacted at 15% when section 7.7 was first introduced in March 1998). For CCPCs, the 10% credit is 100% refundable on up to $1,000,000 of annual eligible expenditures (yielding up to $100,000 in cash refunds), while CCPC expenditures above $1,000,000 and eligible expenditures incurred by non-CCPCs earn a 10% non-refundable credit up to a combined annual expenditure cap of $10,000,000 (with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward). In the 2026–27 Saskatchewan Budget, the provincial government increased funding for Enhancements to the Research and Development Tax Credit program to provide $41 million in annual tax credit benefits across more than 2,700 companies.

In Manitoba, under section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba) (claimed on T2 Schedule 380), corporations with a permanent establishment in Manitoba earn a 15% tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in the province, with no annual expenditure cap. For in-house R&D, 50% of the credit (an effective rate of 7.5%) is refundable in cash and the remaining 50% (7.5%) is non-refundable (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward). Where the eligible R&D is conducted under contract with an eligible Manitoba post-secondary educational or research institution in priority research areas, 100% of the 15% credit is fully refundable.

In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia (under section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), claimed on T2 Schedule 340), New Brunswick (under section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act, claimed on T2 Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (under section 42 of the Income Tax Act, 2000, claimed on T2 Schedule 301) each provide a uniform 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all eligible corporations—regardless of corporate size, CCPC status, foreign ownership, or taxable capital—on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred within the respective province, with no annual expenditure ceiling. Prince Edward Island does not offer a statutory corporate income tax credit for SR&ED, providing innovation support instead through discretionary rebates and grants administered by Innovation PEI. Among the three northern territories, Yukon (claimed on T2 Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Yukon, augmented by an additional 5% refundable bonus credit (for a 20% total refundable credit) on eligible payments made to Yukon University, whereas neither the Northwest Territories nor Nunavut offers a territorial R&D tax credit.
Administrative Governance, Compliance, and Audit Procedures
Governing Authorities and the Dual-Track CRA Review Process

Governance of the federal SR&ED regime is bifurcated between the Department of Finance Canada—which holds exclusive statutory responsibility for tax policy design, legislative drafting, and fiscal consultations—and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers claim intake, risk screening, technical and financial examinations, notices of assessment, and administrative appeals through its SR&ED Directorate.

Upon submission of an SR&ED claim, the CRA subjects the filing to automated and manual risk-assessment screening. Claims accepted as filed without audit are generally processed within the CRA's published service standard of 60 to 120 calendar days from receipt of a complete return. Claims selected for examination undergo a coordinated dual-track review governed by the CRA's Claim Review Manual for Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and Financial Reviewers. On the technical track, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—an in-house science, engineering, or software specialist—evaluates whether each claimed project satisfies the five Northwest Hydraulic questions and the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) by reviewing Form T661 narratives, inspecting contemporaneous engineering artifacts, and conducting interviews with the claimant's lead technical personnel. Simultaneously, on the financial track, a CRA Financial Reviewer audits T4 payroll summaries, time-tracking methodologies, specified employee limitations, arm's-length subcontractor agreements and statements of work, proof of payment within 180 days of year-end under subsection 78(4), capital asset 90% utilization records, and provincial government assistance grinds.

If the RTA or Financial Reviewer proposes to disallow all or part of a claim in a draft SR&ED Review Report, the claimant is afforded 30 days to submit a written rebuttal and supplementary documentation before a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued. Once a Notice of (Re)Assessment is issued, a taxpayer wishing to contest the determination must file a formal Notice of Objection (Form T400A) with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the date of mailing of the Notice, and if the assessment is confirmed or remains unresolved after 90 days, may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada. To provide upfront certainty before R&D capital is deployed, the CRA launched an elective Pre-claim approval process on April 1, 2026, as announced in Budget 2025, under which eligible businesses (CCPCs, other Canadian corporations and Canadian partnerships with annual gross income under $25 million that are in good standing with the CRA) can obtain technical approval of up to three planned SR&ED projects before work starts or costs are incurred, with a determination within eight weeks of a completed application, approval valid for up to three years, and a 90-day (rather than 180-day) processing target for expenditure reviews of claims containing pre-approved projects.
Form T661 Technical Narrative Requirements, Claim Preparer Penalties, and Statutory Deadlines

Strict adherence to the prescribed form and filing deadline rules under subsections 37(11), 127(9), and 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act is a mandatory statutory condition precedent to receiving SR&ED tax incentives. While a corporation's T2 income tax return is due within 6 months after the end of its taxation year, subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) allow a claimant up to 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the qualified expenditures were incurred to file Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) containing the prescribed information. This 18-month reporting deadline operates as an absolute statutory bar: neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada has legal jurisdiction under the fairness/taxpayer relief provisions (subsection 220(3.1)) to waive or extend the 18-month deadline, and any project or expenditure omitted from Form T661 or Schedule 31 as of the 18-month cutoff date is permanently barred from SR&ED deduction and ITC entitlement.

For every project claimed on Form T661, the taxpayer must complete three structured technical narrative fields in Part 2, Section B within strict statutory word limits (as detailed in CRA Guide T4088, Guide to Form T661):
