Furthermore, under subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the Income Tax Act, every claimant must provide complete and accurate Claim Preparer Information on Form T661 disclosing whether an external tax advisor, consultant, or engineering firm assisted in preparing the claim, the billing arrangement code (such as contingency fee percentage, hourly billing, or fixed fee), and the total fee payable. As confirmed by the CRA's T2 Corporation Income Tax Guide (T4012), if a corporation fails to provide complete and accurate claim preparer information, a $1,000 statutory penalty applies under subsection 162(5.1) (for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable), although the underlying SR&ED claim itself will not be disallowed solely because of that omission.
Interaction with Complementary Federal Direct Funding and Patent Box Proposals

Canadian tax law permits claimants to combine ("stack") direct federal and provincial innovation grants, contributions, and concessional loans with SR&ED tax credits, subject to the government assistance reduction rules under subsection 127(9) and program-specific stacking ceilings (generally 75% to 100% of total eligible project costs). The most prominent complementary program for SMEs is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which received renewed clean-technology and commercialization support in Budget 2026 and provides non-repayable contributions covering 50% to 80% of internal technical salaries and contractor costs. When a claimant receives an NRC IRAP grant, only the exact dollar amount of the grant is deducted as government assistance on Line 513 of Form T661; crucially, under Regulation 2900(4), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is still computed on the gross, unreduced SR&ED salary base before deducting the IRAP grant, allowing the claimant to earn both the direct IRAP cash grant and the federal/provincial SR&ED tax credits on the unreimbursed salary plus the full proxy overhead.

For larger commercialization, artificial intelligence, and industrial decarbonization projects, the federal government expanded several direct funding and investment tax credit programs across Budget 2024 and the 2024 Fall Economic Statement. These initiatives include a $2.4 billion investment in artificial intelligence, $150 million over three years starting in 2024–25 for the Global Innovation Clusters, $24 million over two years starting in 2025–26 for the National AI Institutes, $14.5 million over two years starting in 2024–25 to Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) for SME clean-tech intellectual property support, and up to $500 million over four years starting in 2025–26 via the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) to finance SME digital and AI adoption. In parallel, the federal government enacted a suite of refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits—covering Clean Electricity, Clean Hydrogen, Clean Technology Adoption, Clean Technology Manufacturing, Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS), and the Electric Vehicle (EV) Supply Chain (under sections 127.44, 127.45, and 127.48 of the Income Tax Act). Statutory anti-stacking rules prohibit claiming both an SR&ED ITC and a Clean Economy ITC on the exact same capital property expenditure, requiring taxpayers to model and elect the higher-yielding credit at the individual asset level.

Finally, following the federal patent box consultation that concluded on April 15, 2024, the Department of Finance announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and subsequent 2025–2026 budget frameworks its intention to implement a federal patent box regime to incentivize the domestic commercialization and retention of intellectual property developed in Canada. This federal initiative complements existing provincial IP box regimes, including Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations in Québec (IDCI) (which reduces the effective Québec corporate income tax rate on qualified IP income to 2.0%) and Saskatchewan's Commercial Innovation Incentive (which lowers the provincial corporate tax rate to 6.0% for 10 to 15 years on income derived from qualifying patented innovations).
Strategic Audit Synthesis and Compliance Conclusions

The 2024–2026 legislative reforms represent a generational expansion of Canada's R&D tax architecture. By extending the 35% enhanced refundable federal ITC (and the 10% refundable British Columbia SR&ED credit) to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and doubling the annual expenditure limit from $3.0 million to $6.0 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament has removed the structural fiscal cliff that historically penalized Canadian technology companies upon completing a domestic public offering or scaling their R&D budgets. Equally transformative is the enactment of the three-year average gross revenue phase-out election (15M–75M) alongside the widened 15M–75M taxable capital phase-out, which enables capital-intensive, pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPCs to raise large institutional equity or debt rounds without forfeiting their 100% refundable SR&ED tax credits. When combined with the full restoration of capital expenditure eligibility after December 15, 2024, and Québec's consolidation of its provincial R&D incentives into the 30% / 20% refundable CRIC regime covering both R&D and pre-commercialization activities after March 25, 2025, Canada's combined federal-provincial R&D tax subsidy remains among the most generous in the OECD.

To optimize statutory claims while ensuring robust audit defence before the CRA, Revenu Québec, and Alberta TRA, corporate tax directors and R&D auditors should implement five core compliance protocols. First, for every taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million must quantitatively model both the traditional taxable capital phase-out formula and the newly enacted three-year average gross revenue election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), formally electing the gross revenue structure whenever consolidated three-year average revenue yields a higher expenditure limit. Second, to substantiate newly eligible capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024, under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9), taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous machine-hour or operating-time logs proving that the depreciable property satisfies the strict 90% ("all or substantially all") SR&ED utilization threshold, while tracking any subsequent conversion to commercial production to manage ITC recapture exposure under subsections 127(27)–(35).

Third, corporations with establishments in Québec must reconfigure their internal R&D cost-tracking systems for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, to transition from legacy Form RD-1029.7-V to the new CRIC forms (RD-1029.8.CR-T, RD-1029.8.EN-T, and RD-1029.8.PR-T), systematically capturing newly eligible pre-commercialization expenditures (regulatory certification, homologation, industrial product design, and pilot validation) and capital property to maximize the 30% refundable tier on the first $1.0 million and the 20% refundable tier on excess expenditures, while filing on time to avoid the $500/month ($12,000/$24,000 maximum) statutory penalty. Fourth, multi-jurisdictional claimants—particularly those claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant on Form AT29, the Ontario OITC/ORDTC on Schedules 566/508, the BC SR&ED Credit on Form T666, or the Québec CRIC—must accurately execute the two-step provincial government assistance grind on Line 513 of federal Form T661 and evaluate whether waiving non-refundable provincial credits (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC when in a tax-loss position) yields a higher net cash refund at the 35% federal rate. Finally, all Form T661 technical narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246) must be structured strictly in accordance with the judicial standards of Northwest Hydraulic, Les Abeilles, Kam-Press, and Manning Canning—explicitly isolating underlying scientific or technological uncertainties from commercial objectives, documenting chronological hypothesis testing and failed iterations, and linking contemporaneous engineering artifacts directly to the systematic investigation.
